In her address to the General Assembly last September, the President of Slovenia proposed an initiative to seek an advisory opinion of the ICJ on the limitations of the veto power in cases involving genocide and crimes against humanity. The veto carries a particular responsibility, one that the country casting it must be prepared to assume. This is why Slovenia has supported, among other measures, the so-called veto initiative and regularly participates in the general debates they're on. Third, on procedure. We are well aware that divergent views exist within the IGN on the scope and direction of the reform across the five clusters. Such differences are a natural part of any negotiation process. However, the purpose of any process is ultimately to move forward. We therefore believe that actual negotiations should commence based on a text. This means tackling the effectiveness and efficiency of the Council head on, including the question of the veto. The veto must no longer be a shield for impunity or inaction, and it must be a key consideration of reform. The Pact for the Future gives us a political mandate to continue discussions on its limitations. and we must not lose this momentum. But effectiveness alone is not enough. A council that is not representative cannot be legitimate. The Security Council of today reflects the world of 1945, not the world of 2025. It is time to correct this imbalance. Many regions of this world, not least Africa, but also GRULAC and the APG, are severely underrepresented in the Council's current power balance. The historical injustice against Africa must be urgently redressed, as recognized by the Pact for the Future. Excellencies, colleagues, we cannot fail to fulfill our collective commitment under SDG 16.8 to broaden and strengthen the participation of developing countries in global governance. The time for talk has passed. The time for action is now. Austria will continue to remain a constructive and determined partner on reform, and we will support the Co-Chairs in their important work. As in the past, Austria will be guided by the objective to achieve a reform that makes the Council more representative, inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic and accountable. We remain flexible to support any model that garners the broadest possible political support from delegations and lives up to these principles. Allow me to share a few concrete thoughts on the way forward. First, we have built significant political momentum for Security Council reform. The Pact for the Future has moved this debate from aspiration to obligation. The train has left the station. and it must not be allowed to derail. Second, it is now time to operationalize the commitments made by world leaders. We encourage the new co-chairs to use the pact as a political compass and to steer the session toward a consolidated model for reform. Third, we urge all groups and member states that have submitted models to refine and revise them in light of the feedback received. This is how we move from discussion to negotiation. We commend Liechtenstein for taking this step with its revised model and invite others to follow suit. We also commend the CARICOM for submitting a new model during the last session. Fourth, we encourage other major negotiating groups, in particular the African group, to come forward with new models during the session. The voice of Africa must be at the center of this reform. A model from the C-10 would allow for a focused and substantive discussion on Africa's rightful place on the Council. Fifth, we must collectively further the implementation of the interim measures as contained in Action 41 of the Pact for the Future, including the full implementation of Article 27.3 of the UN Charter. As a member of the ACT group, Austria will place particular attention on the implementation of these interim measures. Sixth, we believe that the process should continue to build on best practices of the past and particularly allow space for informal discussions and exchange with civil society. Excellencies, colleagues, this is a moment to match our words with will. Let us not falter in our commitment to this organization, nor in our resolve to make the United Nations truly fit for purpose. I thank you.

President, Excellencies, Malta fully supports the Uniting for Consensus statement delivered at this debate and is making the following remarks in its national capacity. But which direction should reform take us? The UFC has and remains of the view that flexibility will be required throughout the reform process, but certain basic characteristics of our approach remain. We propose to add elected and not permanent seats. We do not support an extension of the veto, and we believe that longer-term reelectable seats would help to ensure stability and Council members who are accountable to the broader UN membership. We believe that this type of reform will best address certain historic injustices, not least that 59 member states, many of them like Malta, small island states, have never served on the Security Council. By focusing on non-permanent seats, the UPC model would allow more countries to serve. There are also pragmatic reasons to prefer new elected seats over new permanent seats. This is also the reason why, as members of the UFC, we argue that any reform of the Council would be strengthened by a new commitment to reduce the use of the veto as much as possible, particularly in cases of alleged mass atrocities and war crimes.
